security_spec.violation_condition: In XiangShan RTL, when the MDCFG Table has an improper setting (non-monotonic MDCFG(m).t values where MDCFG(k).t > MDCFG(m).t for k < m), the IOPMP entry-to-MD assignment logic produces implementation-dependent behavior. If the RTL implements a naive interval-based lookup (e.g., simple combinational comparators without monotonicity enforcement or write-rejection), a transaction with RRID associated to MD_m or MD_k may match entries belonging to an unintended memory domain, or entries may become orphaned and silently grant/deny access contrary to the programmer's intent. This is especially critical when HWCFG0.enable is set after programming improper MDCFG values—the spec now explicitly requires proper settings only when enable is set, creating a window where improper configurations can be latched into working state. The removed reference behaviors (auto-correction, write rejection, entry nullification) are no longer suggested guidance, so if XiangShan adopted or relied on any of those patterns, the RTL must now ensure its custom implementation-dependent behavior still satisfies the two remaining constraints: (a) an entry belongs to at most one MD, and (b) lower-indexed MD entries have lower indices than higher-indexed MD entries.
security_spec.vulnerability_pattern: MDCFG_t_non_monotonic | MDCFG improper setting | MDCFG(m).t comparator unsigned less-than | entry_index_range MDCFG lower_bound upper_bound | HWCFG0_enable MDCFG_proper_setting gate | MDCFG write no monotonicity check
security_spec.summary: PR removes hardware reference behaviors for improper MDCFG Table settings, leaving entry-to-MD assignment purely implementation-dependent; XiangShan RTL without explicit monotonicity enforcement on MDCFG(m).t writes risks entry misattribution across memory domains, enabling unauthorized memory access through RRID-to-MD association bypass

findings.finding: MDCFG write path has no monotonicity check. Writes to MDCFG(m).t are unconditionally accepted into SRAM (mdcfg.io.a_we := true.B when io.regcfg.v && io.regcfg.rw). No comparison is made against MDCFG(m-1).t or MDCFG(m+1).t to detect or reject non-monotonic settings. When an improper (non-monotonic) MDCFG table is written, the Ctrl FSM will use these values directly in its interval-scan logic, leading to implementation-dependent behavior that may not satisfy spec requirements (a) entry belongs to at most one MD, (b) lower-indexed MD entries have lower indices.

spec_citations.excerpt: Programmers should maintain proper settings in the MDCFG Table when HWCFG0.enable is set, where MDCFG(m + 1).t should be greater than or equal to MDCFG(m).t for any legal MD m. Otherwise, the MDCFG table has an improper setting... When the MDCFG Table has an improper setting, the resulting association of IOPMP entries to MDs is implementation-dependent, but the following conditions must be held: an entry must belong to at most one memory domain; and the index of an entry in a lower-indexed memory domain must be lower than that in a higher-indexed memory domain.

Field t [15:0] WARL: Indicate the encoding the range of memory domain m. An IOPMP entry with index j belongs to MD m: If MDCFG(m-1).t ≤ j < MDCFG(m).t, where m > 0. If j < MDCFG(0).t where m = 0. If MDCFG(m-1).t > MDCFG(m).t, then MDCFG Table is improperly programmed.

findings.finding: sPriority exit condition uses simple equality (j_indx === md_t) with j_indx initialized from md_t_pre and monotonically incrementing. When MDCFG is non-monotonic (md_t_pre > md_t), j_indx starts above md_t and increments past it without matching. The FSM then scans entries beyond the intended MD boundary—j_indx wraps through all 65536 values before eventually equaling md_t. During this scan, entries nominally belonging to other MDs (or beyond entry_num=512) are checked against the current MD's RRID, potentially matching entries from wrong memory domains. This violates the spec-guaranteed constraint that entries belong to at most one MD.

spec_citations.excerpt: When the MDCFG Table has an improper setting, the resulting association of IOPMP entries to MDs is implementation-dependent, but the following conditions must be held: an entry must belong to at most one memory domain; and the index of an entry in a lower-indexed memory domain must be lower than that in a higher-indexed memory domain.

findings.finding: j_indx is initialized to md_t_pre (line 1219) and incremented unconditionally (line 1221) without any upper-bound check against HWCFG1.entry_num (512). j_indx and md_t/md_t_pre are all 16-bit registers, allowing software to program MDCFG(m).t values up to 65535. When md_t exceeds entry_num, the FSM scans non-existent entries (j_indx >= entry_num), which are spec-defined as OFF/not-available. Combined with non-monotonic settings, this amplifies the boundary-violation behavior.

spec_citations.excerpt: an entry with index j belongs to MD m if MDCFG(m - 1).t ≤ j < MDCFG(m).t, where m > 0. an entry with index j belongs to MD 0 if j < MDCFG(0).t.

findings.finding: HWCFG0.enable is set via W1SS (reg_hwcfg0.enable | w.enable) without any validation of the MDCFG table state. There is no monotonicity gate or warning mechanism that checks whether MDCFG entries are properly programmed before enabling transaction checking. Since the write path (lines 328-330) also lacks monotonicity enforcement, improper MDCFG settings can be silently latched into the working configuration and activated by setting enable.

spec_citations.excerpt: Programmers should maintain proper settings in the MDCFG Table when HWCFG0.enable is set

findings.finding: md_t and md_t_pre are read from the MDCFG SRAM in two consecutive FSM cycles (sMdcfg then sMdcfgPre). A concurrent MDCFG register write (via APB/RegCfg on Port A of TrueDualPortSRAM) between these two reads can change the relationship between md_t and md_t_pre. The stall signal (line 1356: io.regcfg.v && io.regcfg.rw) only gates the sSrcmd→sMdcfg transition (line 1093), not sMdcfg→sMdcfgPre. If a write modifies MDCFG(m).t between the two reads, the FSM may use a stale md_t_pre or md_t value, creating a window where a momentarily non-monotonic pair is used.
findings.snippet:
when(state === State.sMdcfg && md_hasTask) { // if have undone md task, read md.t
    md_taskIdx_d := md_taskIdx
    io.mdcfg.m_indx := md_taskIdx
    io.mdcfg.m_en := true.B
}.elsewhen(state === State.sMdcfgPre && md_taskIdx_d =/= 0.U) { // read pre md.t
    io.mdcfg.m_indx := md_taskIdx_d - 1.U
    io.mdcfg.m_en := true.B
}

findings.finding: All configuration protection registers (MDCFGLCK, MDLCK, MDLCKH, ENTRYLCK) are entirely commented out. The spec (chapter3) defines these as the hardware mechanism to lock MDCFG Table entries, SRCMD Table MD associations, and Entry Array entries against runtime modification. Without these locks, there is no hardware-enforced configuration integrity. A compromised software component can rewrite MDCFG, SRCMD, or entry registers at any time with no hardware-level defense.

spec_citations.excerpt: Register MDCFGLCK is designed to partially or fully lock the MDCFG Table... MDCFG(m) is locked if m < MDCFGLCK.f. MDCFGLCK.f is incremental-only... If MDCFG(m) is locked for MD m, all its preceding MDCFG Table entries (MDCFG(0) to MDCFG(m-1)) must also be locked.

locked entries should be placed in the higher priorities. Otherwise, when the secure monitor is compromised, one unlocked entry in higher priority can override the effects of all the other locked or non-locked entries in lower priority.

findings.finding: The RegCfgMux performs correct address-range-based demultiplexing of APB register writes to the MDCFG, SRCMD, entry, and info register tables. Address decode uses combinatorial comparators against base and max addresses, which is correct. The Mux unconditionally forwards writes based on address match—this is correct behavior for an address demux; write qualification is the responsibility of the downstream module (RegMap for info registers, MdcfgTable for MDCFG). The issue is that MdcfgTable itself does not qualify writes (see finding 1).
findings.snippet:
regcfgs.foreach { case (regcfg, hit) =>
  regcfg.rw   := Mux(hit, io.regcfg.rw, false.B)
  regcfg.addr := Mux(hit, io.regcfg.addr, 0.U)
  regcfg.din  := Mux(hit, io.regcfg.din, 0.U)
  regcfg.v    := Mux(hit, io.regcfg.v, false.B)
}

findings.finding: The HWCFG0 register bit layout is correct. The toUInt concatenation (line 516) matches the spec-defined field ordering: enable at bit 31, addrh_en at bit 30, md_num at bits 29:24, md_entry_num at bits 23:17, followed by feature-indication bits. All read-only fields are correctly initialized from IopmpParams. The enable field is correctly initialized to 0 and uses W1SS semantics (line 806). md_entry_num is correctly set to 0 for mdcfg_fmt=0 as required by the spec.
findings.snippet: def toUInt: UInt = Cat(enable, addrh_en, md_num, md_entry_num, mfr_en, pees, peis, stall_en, no_w, no_x, chk_x, rrid_transl_prog, rrid_transl_en, prient_prog, user_cfg_en, sps_en, tor_en, srcmd_fmt, mdcfg_fmt)
